title: Monitor the temperature of food products and their environment for quality control purposes

lessons.title: Why temperature control matters in meat
lessons.html:
Temperature is a food safety control

Fresh meat is a perfect place for bacteria to grow. It is moist, rich in protein and has a near-neutral pH. The single most powerful tool an abattoir or meat plant has to slow bacteria down is temperature. As a meat examiner or quality controller you must understand why temperature is checked, not only how.

The danger zone

Most food-poisoning bacteria such as Salmonella, E. coli and Staphylococcus aureus grow fastest between roughly 5 °C and 60 °C. This range is commonly called the danger zone. Inside it, bacteria can double in number in as little as 20 minutes. Below it, growth slows down a great deal; when meat is frozen, growth stops but the bacteria are not killed. Above about 60 °C, most bacteria start to die, which is why cooking and hot holding work.

What temperature affects

  • Safety – fast growth of pathogens can make consumers ill.
  • Shelf life – spoilage bacteria cause slime, off-odours and discolouration, so warm meat must be sold or discarded sooner.
  • Eating quality – chilling a carcass too fast or too slowly affects tenderness and colour. For example, very rapid chilling of warm muscle can cause cold shortening and tough meat.
  • Weight – poor chiller conditions increase drip and evaporation loss, which costs the plant money.

Product and environment

You must monitor two things. The product temperature is the temperature inside the meat itself, usually measured at the deepest part (the core). The environment temperature is the air in chillers, freezers, cutting rooms, dispatch bays and refrigerated trucks. A chiller with cold air does not guarantee cold meat: if carcasses are packed too tightly or loaded while still warm, the core can stay in the danger zone for many hours.

Where the limits come from

Every registered abattoir and meat plant in South Africa works under the Meat Safety Act 40 of 2000 and its regulations, and most run a HACCP (Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Point) system. Your plant's HACCP plan sets the exact critical limits for chilling, cutting rooms and dispatch. Always work to the limits written in your plant's procedures, and ask your supervisor or the veterinary officials if you are unsure.

lessons.title: Measuring temperature correctly
lessons.html:
Instruments and how to use them

A temperature reading is only useful if it is accurate and taken in the right place. Poor technique gives false comfort and can let unsafe meat leave the plant.

Types of instruments

InstrumentUse
Digital probe thermometerCore temperature of carcasses, cuts and mince
Fixed room sensor or data loggerContinuous air temperature in chillers and freezers
Infrared (surface) thermometerQuick surface checks on deliveries; it does not read the core
Truck data loggerTemperature record during transport

Taking a core reading

  1. Clean and sanitise the probe before and after every product, so you do not spread bacteria from one carcass to another.
  2. Insert the probe into the thickest part of the meat, for example deep in the hindquarter (the round) of a beef carcass, without touching bone.
  3. Wait until the reading is stable before recording it.
  4. Check several carcasses in different positions in the chiller: near the door, in the middle and at the back. The warmest point tells you the most.

Checking the instrument

Thermometers drift over time, so they must be checked (verified) regularly against a known reference. A common check is the ice-point test: put the probe into a mixture of crushed ice and a little clean water, stir, and the thermometer should read 0 °C. Some plants also compare their probes with a calibrated reference thermometer. If a thermometer is outside the tolerance in your procedure, label it, remove it from use and report it. Record every verification with the date, the instrument number and your signature.

Common mistakes

  • Measuring only the surface of a thick cut.
  • Reading too quickly, before the display has settled.
  • Only checking the carcasses nearest the chiller door.
  • Using a dirty probe or one with a flat battery.
  • Trusting the chiller wall display without ever checking it against a hand-held thermometer.

lessons.title: Recording, reporting and corrective action
lessons.html:
From reading to decision

Monitoring is not finished when you read the thermometer. You must record what you found, compare it with the limit, and act if something is wrong.

Keeping records

Temperature records are legal and quality evidence. Inspectors and auditors use them to see that the plant is in control. A good record shows:

  • the date and time of the check;
  • the place (for example Chiller 2, dispatch bay, truck registration number);
  • the product or carcass number checked;
  • the reading, written exactly as measured, never rounded to look better;
  • any corrective action taken; and
  • the name and signature of the person who checked.

Write in pen, do not use correction fluid, and if you make a mistake draw a single line through it and initial it. Never fill in readings later from memory.

When a reading is out of limit

  1. Report at once to your supervisor or the quality controller.
  2. Hold the product: mark it and keep it separate so it is not dispatched until a decision is made.
  3. Find the cause: is the chiller door left open, is the refrigeration unit iced up, is the chiller overloaded, or were warm carcasses loaded too late in the day?
  4. Fix the cause with maintenance or the production team.
  5. Decide on the product: the responsible person, often with the veterinary official, decides whether it can be re-chilled, must be processed quickly, or must be condemned.
  6. Record everything that was done.

Example

At 06:00 you find the core temperature of beef carcasses at the back of Chiller 3 above the plant limit, while those near the door are fine. You see the evaporator fan at the back is not turning. You report it, the carcasses are held, maintenance repairs the fan, and the carcasses are re-checked every hour until they reach the limit. All of this is written on the chiller log.

Key points

  • Bacteria grow fastest in the danger zone of about 5 °C to 60 °C.
  • Monitor both the product core and the air around it.
  • Clean the probe, measure the thickest part and wait for a stable reading.
  • Verify thermometers regularly, for example with the ice-point test.
  • Record readings honestly and act at once when a limit is exceeded.
